newsitem.title: UK: Analyst sees hi-tech boom in copper use.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees hi-tech boom in copper use.

text.p: As world industrial activity becomes more high-tech it tends to need much more copper, specialists Bloomsbury Minerals Economics (BME) said a study.
In a detailed analysis of the intensity of copper usage from 1990 to 1995, BME found that only Japan did not follow this trend among nations of the developed world.
"It's a question of Japanese industry hollowing out... moving to offshore plants," analyst Peter Holland told Reuters.
During the five-year period, Japanese industrial output fell by 1.8 percent per year.
But the finding that the rest of the developed world stepped up its use of copper was a surprise, Hollands said.

"Sharply rising intensity of use of copper semis per unit of industrial production seems not to be confined to the USA as BME earlier thought; rather it seems common to most of the developed world, Japan being a notable exception," he said in the report.
"BME suspects that it is an enduring and very fundamental feature of the present era that as industrial activity becomes more high-tech, it becomes dramatically more copper intensive," Hollands said.
"The implications for refined copper consumption look very positive," he added.
With a raft of new mines coming on stream, most analysts project a copper surplus swamping the market in coming years.
"It now appears we will have a much more forgiving environment...any surplus will take less time to work off," Hollands said in the interview.
In the next monthly report, BME will almost certainly have to raise copper consumption growth forecasts for the US and Europe, he added.
In the United States, total production of semi-fabricated copper and alloy (semis) rose by 4.9 percent and total semis consumption by 5.0 percent each year from 1990 to 1995.
Intensity of use in industrial production has been rising at 2.4 percent per year for semis production and 2.5 percent for total copper and alloy semis consumption during the same period.

In Europe, France, Germany, Italy and Britain have seen rising intensities of use in industrial production for total copper semis production of 2.3 percent, 2.9 percent, 4.2 percent and 3.7 percent annually during the five-year period respectively.

But in Japan, copper intensity of use in industrial production for total semis output only increased by 0.1 percent per year and fell by 1.2 percent for semis consumption. --Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8065
